When Can LLM Reasoning Reliably
Reuse Intermediate Results?

Deyuan Liu Affiliation: Westlake University    Zecheng Wang Affiliation: Wechat AI    Xuanyi Liu Affiliation: Peking University    Jungang Li Affiliation: HKUST    Yihao Hu Affiliation: Westlake University Affiliation: Ant Group    Mingjie Tang Affiliation: IQuest Research    Bryan Dai Affiliation: IQuest Research    Jie Fu ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: IQuest Research
Abstract

Sampling complete solutions gives large language models more chances to solve a problem, but each attempt starts again. For tasks with several subproblems, all required answers must be correct in the same attempt. Retaining intermediate results can avoid repeating correct work, but errors in those results may affect later attempts. We study when this reuse is reliable and how much computation it requires. For local retries that stop when no candidate passes within the retry budget, we give conditions for correct completion and bound the average number of attempts. We also show how checking cost and the chance of passing a check affect total computation. Experiments across eight reasoning models examine composite mathematics and arithmetic. Across four DeepSeek models, average success on the second subproblem is 36.2 percent without first-subproblem context, 57.2 percent with its answer, and 58.3 percent with its reasoning and answer. These scores measure second-subproblem coverage and include continuations made when selection fails. Arithmetic experiments show that similar first-attempt accuracies can lead to very different coverage after repeated attempts. Code is available at https://github.com/SempraETY/Intermediate-State-Reuse.

1 Introduction

Many practical reasoning tasks require several distinct subproblems to be solved together. Solving each subproblem in isolation does not ensure that a model can solve the complete task (Zhang et al., 2025b). With model weights fixed, a system can spend more computation at inference time to improve its chance of finding a solution. A system can generate more complete answers, compare candidates, or check intermediate work (Brown et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2024). How this computation is allocated matters alongside how much is available (Snell et al., 2025).

Under complete-solution sampling, all required subproblem answers must be correct in one run. One run may solve the first subproblem and another the second, while neither solves both. The sample pool contains correct answers to both subproblems, but no run has solved the complete task. As tasks get longer, more intermediate work can be lost when an attempt fails near the end. A restart retries the failed subproblem but repeats earlier work that may already be correct. Existing methods already use intermediate work: Least-to-Most prompting solves subproblems in sequence using earlier answers (Zhou et al., 2023), while Tree of Thoughts searches over partial reasoning states (Yao et al., 2023).

A subproblem may contain several reasoning steps; our analysis uses steps whose intermediate states can be checked and retained. Consider a three-step calculation that derives a formula, substitutes the given values, and computes a final quantity. Suppose the first two steps are correct but the final calculation fails. A complete restart generates all three steps again. If the formula and substitution can be checked and retained, a new attempt can repeat only the final calculation. The retained results become the retry’s input.

The difficulty is deciding what can safely be kept. A check may reject a correct candidate or accept an incorrect one; benchmarks document the difficulty of identifying errors in intermediate reasoning (Zheng et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025). An error passed forward may then affect later attempts, as studies of self-conditioning illustrate (Sinha et al., 2025). Even a correct intermediate answer may leave out assumptions or other information needed to continue. Atom of Thoughts constructs self-contained reasoning states (Teng et al., 2025), while MEM1 learns to retain compact information across interaction steps (Zhou et al., 2025). Keeping a full reasoning trace instead supplies more context, but may also retain unchecked mistakes and increases the context to process. Checking itself consumes computation, so avoiding a restart does not by itself establish a saving. This report studies the conditions under which intermediate results can be reused reliably and the cost of doing so.

Recent search methods also avoid unnecessary branching: Chain-in-Tree continues routine steps sequentially and reuses generated children when branching is needed (Li, 2026). Process supervision evaluates intermediate reasoning (Lightman et al., 2024), and MAKER combines fine-grained decomposition with voting to execute long deterministic tasks (Meyerson et al., 2025). MAKER derives near-linear expected computation under its voting model, including the cost of discarded responses. We consider finite local retries, where the first candidate to pass a check is retained and may carry an error into later steps.

The analyzed procedure checks each new result and retries from the last retained state after a rejection. It stops when every candidate within the local budget is rejected. For fixed generation and checking, retries reduce exhaustion without improving the reliability of accepted states. We give an attainable reliability bound and matching worst-case bounds on expected attempts. The work bound includes paths after an incorrect acceptance, where correct-prefix acceptance guarantees no longer apply. Exhaustion limits the work spent at frequently rejected states. Sufficient precision and acceptance probability yield linear expected attempts; total cost also includes checking and state processing.

We also report sampling experiments across eight reasoning models. Arithmetic tasks let us ask how much repeated attempts add beyond first-attempt accuracy. Pairs of mathematics problems let us compare candidate selection and the context supplied to the second subproblem: no first-subproblem context, its answer alone, or its reasoning and answer. The paired subproblems are mathematically separate. Their continuation prompts differ in both content and instructions, so the comparison concerns entire prompt configurations. Budget sweeps examine how success and generated tokens change when more computation is spent on first-subproblem candidates or subsequent continuations.

Across four DeepSeek models, second-subproblem success is 36.2% without first-subproblem context, 57.2% with its answer, and 58.3% with its reasoning and answer. Paired uncertainty is unavailable for these prompt comparisons. These scores include fallback continuations and measure success on the second subproblem, rather than joint success of both answers. Arithmetic results show that similar first-attempt accuracies can lead to very different coverage after repeated attempts. A separate EdgeBench study compares two curves for predicting later agent scores from early observations and observations of the same agents on other tasks (Zhu et al., 2026).

Report overview.

  1. (a)

    Reliability of reuse. We give an attainable trajectory bound and the exact accepted-state error threshold for a finite cap to guarantee target reliability.

  2. (b)

    Expected work and checking cost. We bound worst-case expected work, including erroneous paths, and connect reliable completion to acceptance probability and attempt cost.

  3. (c)

    Empirical findings. We compare retries, answer selection, retained context, and budget allocation across eight reasoning models, and evaluate two curves for predicting later agent scores.

2 Preliminaries

We first define complete-task success, the state passed between steps, and the sampling metrics. These definitions distinguish finding a complete answer from continuing successfully after an intermediate result.

2.1 Tasks, States, and Sampling Metrics

A composite task x1⊕x2x_{1}\oplus x_{2} presents two subproblems in one prompt and is correct only when both returned subproblem answers are correct. Let a⋆​(x)a^{\star}(x) be the target answer to xx, with a⋆​(x1⊕x2)=[a⋆​(x1),a⋆​(x2)]a^{\star}(x_{1}\oplus x_{2})=[a^{\star}(x_{1}),a^{\star}(x_{2})]. Let 𝜽\bm{\theta} denote the model parameters and p𝜽(⋅∣s)p_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot\mid s) its distribution over generated text under a fixed decoding configuration and input context ss. For a problem xx, fix a decomposition into N≥1N\geq 1 steps, where NN counts the steps in this chosen decomposition. Write ztz_{t} for the text generated at step t∈{1,…,N}t\in\{1,\ldots,N\} and st=[x,z1,…,zt]s_{t}=[x,z_{1},\ldots,z_{t}] for the resulting state, with s0=xs_{0}=x. Each step is sampled from p𝜽(⋅∣st−1)p_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot\mid s_{t-1}). For reuse, sts_{t} denotes the state actually passed forward: task information plus retained generated text or extracted intermediate answers. The prompt specifies how this state is presented to the model. Correctness concerns the information carried forward; a correct extracted answer need not imply that discarded reasoning was correct. We call a task stepwise decomposable if it can be split into steps whose intermediate states admit a task-specific accept-or-reject check. A state is accepted if it passes the check; acceptance need not imply correctness. A stage groups steps, such as those used to solve one subproblem. Let yy be the final answer extracted from a completed run and LL its total number of generated tokens. The single-run metrics are:

A𝜽,1​(x)=P⁡(y=a⋆​(x)),C𝜽,1​(x)=𝔼⁡[L].A_{\bm{\theta},1}(x)=P\!\left(y=a^{\star}(x)\right),\qquad C_{\bm{\theta},1}(x)=\mathbb{E}[L]. (1)

2.2 Complete-Solution Sampling

In a common pool of composite runs, joint success implies that each subproblem is covered, while separately correct subproblem answers may occur in different runs (Prop. 2). If standalone and composite subproblem marginals agree at a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1), with independence within and across runs, then for K≥2K\geq 2,

1−(1−a1​a2)K\displaystyle 1-(1-a_{1}a_{2})^{K} <[1−(1−a1)K]\displaystyle<[1-(1-a_{1})^{K}] (3)
⋅[1−(1−a2)K].\displaystyle\cdot[1-(1-a_{2})^{K}].

One run must solve both subproblems, whereas separate coverage can use different runs. This sampling constraint also applies to other stochastic solvers; it does not equate token costs across prompt formats. Under the additional assumptions of exponentially declining complete-run accuracy and linear generation cost (Zhang et al., 2025b), complete restarts require exponentially growing generation cost at fixed reliability. Appendix B.8 gives the product comparison, numerical example, and scaling calculation. We next examine the reliability and cost of retaining intermediate work.

3 Reliability and Cost of State Reuse

The reuse loop maintains one accepted state at a time. We analyze the probability that every retained state is correct, the number of executed attempts, and the resulting computational cost.

3.1 Local Retries and Reliable Completion

At step tt, generate a candidate from the retained state st−1✓s_{t-1}^{\checkmark} and check the state to be passed forward. Let 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} indicate acceptance and 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} its correctness. Retain the first accepted state; if all RR attempts are rejected, terminate the entire task. Conditional on the complete history at entry to each reached step, attempts are independent and identically distributed, including at incorrect inputs. Rejected candidates do not change the state or retry law; different steps may depend on earlier accepted results. Checking an extracted answer does not establish that a retained reasoning trace is also correct.

At a correct entry history ss, let ρt​(s)\rho_{t}(s) be the rejection probability and wt​(s)w_{t}(s) the probability of incorrect acceptance in one attempt. Assume ρt​(s)≤ρ∈[0,1)\rho_{t}(s)\leq\rho\in[0,1) and accepted-state error αt​(s)≤α∈[0,1)\alpha_{t}(s)\leq\alpha\in[0,1) at every correct entry history. Conditioning on the first acceptance gives

αt​(R,s)=wt​(s)1−ρt​(s)=αt​(s).\alpha_{t}(R;s)=\frac{w_{t}(s)}{1-\rho_{t}(s)}=\alpha_{t}(s). (4)

Accepted-state precision is 1−αt​(s)1-\alpha_{t}(s); it does not improve with RR. The local trajectory fails if the retry budget is exhausted or an incorrect candidate is accepted:

βt​(R,s)\displaystyle\beta_{t}(R;s) =ρt​(s)R\displaystyle=\rho_{t}(s)^{R} (5)
+(1−ρt​(s)R)​αt​(s).\displaystyle+\bigl(1-\rho_{t}(s)^{R}\bigr)\alpha_{t}(s).

More retries reduce exhaustion; improving accepted-state precision requires a different generation or checking rule. Let HtH_{t} mean that the first tt steps complete with every retained state correct, with H0H_{0} certain. Assume HNH_{N} yields the target answer; later repair can also succeed outside HNH_{N}.

Each correct prefix advances correctly with conditional probability at least (1−ρR)​(1−α)(1-\rho^{R})(1-\alpha); the chain rule gives the product without independence between steps. A homogeneous process with irreversible errors after acceptance attains it. At equality in Eq. (7), the target is approached only with unbounded retries; for ρ=0\rho=0, equality is allowed and one attempt suffices. This is a worst-case guarantee, not a necessary precision threshold for every system that can repair errors. Appendix B.10.1 gives the proof, exact minimum cap, and the simpler sufficient allocation N​α<δN\alpha<\delta used in Prop. 4.

3.2 Expected Work under the Stopping Rule

We measure work by WW, the number of executed candidate attempts. The pathwise cap W≤N​RW\leq NR reserves the full budget at every step. Actual work can be smaller because a step ends as soon as a candidate passes. Let 𝒫N,R\mathcal{P}_{N,R} contain all processes following the preceding retry and stopping rules for at most NN steps, with arbitrary history-dependent rejection probabilities and no correctness requirement. If acceptance were at least h>0h>0 at every reached state, the geometric waiting-time bound would give 𝔼⁡[W]≤N/h\mathbb{E}[W]\leq N/h directly. After an incorrect acceptance, the process may reach states where the correct-prefix acceptance bound no longer holds. The next theorem includes work at these states.

Frequently rejected states are expensive to leave but likely to exhaust the cap, ending the run. The proof uses this tradeoff to bound their expected visits; a homogeneous process gives the matching lower bound (Appendix B.10.3). That lower bound concerns the unrestricted class, not every reliable process. The stopping pattern is related to classical start-up demonstration tests (Gera, 2013). Appendix B.10.6 gives the exact dynamic recursion and separates this uniform bound from fixed-law waiting-time calculations. Together with Thm. 1, this yields reliable completion with an O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) cap and linear expected work. Here the target failure probability is fixed, acceptance at correct prefixes has a positive constant lower bound, and accepted-state error decreases with chain length as specified in Cor. 1.

Example: reserved budget and executed work.

For 100 steps, a cap of 12 attempts reserves at most 1,200 attempts. Suppose every reached state has rejection probability 1/21/2, and every correct prefix has accepted-state error at most 0.00020.0002. The reliability bound exceeds 0.9560.956, while each reached step uses fewer than two attempts in expectation, giving fewer than 200 over the task. The probabilities in this example are hypothetical. The example distinguishes the reserved budget from expected work; Thm. 2 additionally permits arbitrary rejection probabilities after an incorrect acceptance.

3.3 Checking Precision and Computation

As a chain grows, the reliability bound requires a smaller error rate among accepted states. Reaching this precision may make checking more expensive or cause it to reject more candidates. Let hNh_{N} lower-bound acceptance probability at every correct prefix, and let gNg_{N} uniformly bound per-attempt cost, including generation, checking, and state processing at every reached state.

The cap controls exhaustion; Thm. 2 bounds all executed attempts, including those after an incorrect acceptance (Appendix B.10.4). For constant hNh_{N}, expected attempts are linear, whereas the deterministic cost cap remains O⁡(N​log⁡N​gN)O(N\log N\,g_{N}). Since W≥N​𝟏HNW\geq N\mathbf{1}_{H_{N}} and 𝔼⁡[W∣HN]≤𝔼⁡[W]/(1−δ)\mathbb{E}[W\mid H_{N}]\leq\mathbb{E}[W]/(1-\delta), this conclusion is compatible with reliable completion, rather than relying only on cheap failures.

At a common precision target, the relevant cost scale is gN/hNg_{N}/h_{N}. Under independent binary checks, requiring unanimity can make acceptance polynomially rare, yielding Θ⁡(N1+γ​log⁡N)\Theta(N^{1+\gamma}\log N) expected cost for some γ>0\gamma>0 when every check is executed. With an additional separation condition, majority checking keeps acceptance bounded away from zero and gives O⁡(N​log⁡N)O(N\log N) expected cost (Hoeffding, 1963). Appendix B.10.5 specifies the noise model and derives both cases; these repeatedly check one candidate rather than compare different answers by self-consistency.

The work bound relies on the execution rule: feedback-dependent retries or continuation after exhaustion can each use N​RNR attempts. The experiments below use batch selection, multiple continuations, and fallback with different success criteria. They do not directly test these guarantees.

4 Experiments

We compare coverage across budgets, selection rules, and continuation prompts. The tasks cover composite mathematics, complete-answer arithmetic retries, and agent-score prediction.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Models and tasks.

We evaluate DeepSeek-R1-Distill (1.5B, 7B, 8B, 14B) (Guo et al., 2025), Qwen3-Thinking (4B, 30B-A3B) (Team, 2025), and GPT-OSS (20B, 120B) (OpenAI, 2025). LoRe-Compo contains 250 pairs of distinct-subject MATH500 problems, using each of the 500 subproblems once (Zhang et al., 2025b; Hendrycks et al., 2021). The second subproblem is a separate mathematical problem that does not require the first answer. Arithmetic uses 50 problems for each base (7 or 10), operation (addition or multiplication), and digit count n∈{1,…,10}n\in\{1,\ldots,10\}, with 32 complete-answer attempts per problem.

Procedures and success criteria.

Composite Pass@KK requires both correct answers in one of KK complete runs. The two-stage protocol instead generates MM answers to x1x_{1}, retains at most BB candidates, and continues on x2x_{2}. Oracle selects reference-matching answers; self-consistency (SC) uses the modal answer when its vote share reaches 0.5. If selection returns none, fallback candidates are retained for continuation. Both procedures generate whole subproblem answers without checking individual reasoning steps.

The reported second-subproblem success rate A2retA_{2}^{\mathrm{ret}} counts any correct answer to x2x_{2} among the retained continuations, including fallbacks and regardless of x1x_{1} correctness. Joint retained-path success would require both answers to be correct along one shared path, with all 250 pairs still in the denominator. Thus A2retA_{2}^{\mathrm{ret}} upper-bounds joint coverage but does not determine it. It measures coverage, not final-answer selection accuracy. The theoretical loop returns one first-accepted state and stops at exhaustion; the experimental protocol uses multiple continuations and fallback. Appendix C.2 defines these events.

Sampling, matching, and cost.

All mathematical generations have a 10,240-token cap. A composite run shares this cap across two answers, whereas staged solving grants one cap per subproblem. LoRe-Compo uses family-specific decoding settings and direct prompt strings without model-specific chat templates. Decoding differs between Pass@1 and larger budgets, some Pass@1 values come from prior work, and cross-budget nesting is unspecified for the composite results. Answer matching uses numeric tolerance or normalized strings, with separate extraction rules for single and paired answers (Appendix C.1). We report recorded generated-token counts and success percentage points per thousand tokens. Equal attempt counts allow different generation budgets. The token counts exclude some checking and state processing costs and are not matched for whole-task reliability.

4.2 Complete-Solution Sampling on Composite Tasks

Table 2 reports joint composite Pass@KK. The eight-model mean is 8.2% at K=1K=1 and 33.3% at the largest recorded budget (K=32K=32 for R1-1.5B and K=128K=128 otherwise). Coverage improves across these endpoint configurations, but the gains and model ordering vary. Qwen3-4B starts at 4.8%, below R1-8B at 13.2%, and reaches 38.0% compared with 37.2% at K=128K=128. GPT-OSS-120B has the highest Pass@1 and Pass@128, at 19.6% and 38.4%. Model rankings depend on the sampling budget.

GPT-OSS-20B changes from 34.8% at K=8K=8 to 33.2% at K=32K=32. Because nesting and decoding are not held fixed across all configurations, this decrease does not show that adding samples to an unchanged pool reduces coverage. The table reports how often a complete run answers both subproblems correctly. Measuring unused partial success requires the statistic in Appendix C.2.

4.3 Candidate Selection and Retained Context

Intermediate-answer selection.

Table 2 compares Oracle and SC at M=8M=8, B=4B=4 using the same second-subproblem criterion. The four-DeepSeek SC mean is 57.9%; across all eight models, SC and Oracle differ by at most 1.6 percentage points. Here, Oracle and SC yield similar second-subproblem success despite using different selection rules. These scores include fallback continuations, so they do not show that the selectors retain equally accurate first answers. The subproblems are mathematically separate, so a wrong first answer need not prevent success on the second.

The reported SC-to-Pass@8 generated-token ratios are approximately 1.01–1.12 for R1-1.5B, R1-7B, R1-14B, and GPT-OSS-20B, and 1.4–1.5 for the other models. These procedures use different success criteria, so the ratios cannot establish savings at matched whole-task success rates.

Continuation-prompt configurations.

At the same continuation budget, the four-DeepSeek means are 36.2% for no_context, 57.2% for answer_only, and 58.3% for full_context (Table 3). The answer-only prompt scores 21.0 percentage points above no context; full context scores another 1.1 points higher. This small gap does not establish that the two prompts are equivalent. The answer-only mean matches the Oracle mean in Table 2; the SC mean reported above is a separate result. The available prompt-comparison summary does not identify the selector configuration.

The prompts differ in instructions as well as content; these scores compare complete configurations and do not isolate the contribution of the first answer. The answer-only protocol retains the same extracted answer assessed during selection, whereas full context also retains an unchecked reasoning trace truncated to fit the context budget.

How candidate and continuation budgets trade off.

Table 4 compares four tested allocations. Its (8,4)(8,4) success column reproduces the Oracle column of Table 2; the aggregate table alone does not identify the selector used for every other allocation. The eight-model mean rises from 52.8% at 36.4K tokens for (4,2)(4,2) to 56.3% at 72.3K for (8,4)(8,4), a 3.5-point gain for approximately twice the generation. Moving to (16,8)(16,8) gives 57.4% at 144.5K, another 1.1 points for approximately twice the tokens again. The second budget expansion yields a smaller gain in success. We use (8,4)(8,4) as an intermediate reference; (4,2)(4,2) has higher success per thousand generated tokens.

The intermediate allocations separate changes in candidate count from changes in continuation count. At B=2B=2, increasing MM from 4 to 8 raises mean success by 1.7 points, from 52.8% to 54.5%, for 27.0K additional tokens. At M=8M=8, increasing BB from 2 to 4 raises mean success by 1.8 points, from 54.5% to 56.3%, for 8.9K additional tokens. Increasing the continuation budget therefore gives a similar mean gain with fewer additional generated tokens in this comparison.

The model-level responses also vary. At M=8M=8, raising BB from 2 to 4 changes R1-8B from 44.8% to 51.2%, while GPT-OSS-120B stays at 62.4%. GPT-OSS-20B changes from 48.4% to 47.2%; without nested pools this cannot be attributed to keeping more candidates. Across (4,2)(4,2) to (8,4)(8,4), R1-8B gains 10.0 points, compared with 0.4 points each for R1-7B and GPT-OSS-120B. The gains therefore depend on both the model and the allocation of the sampling budget.

Resolution of the comparisons.

With 250 pairs per model, one changed pair corresponds to 0.4 percentage points. The largest SC–Oracle difference is a net difference of four successful pairs. Paired uncertainty is unavailable for these comparisons and for the 1.1-point full-context increment, so we interpret the figures as descriptive comparisons of the evaluated configurations.

4.4 Finite-Budget Arithmetic Retries

The arithmetic experiments ask how many initially missed problems can be solved with more attempts. Here the candidate is an entire arithmetic answer, not a checked digit-level state. We write E^​(R)\hat{E}(R) for the fraction of problems with no correct answer among their first RR attempts; empirical Pass@RR is 1−E^​(R)1-\hat{E}(R). The checkpoints use prefixes of the same pool of 32 complete-answer attempts.

Across 320 model–base–operation–digit conditions, 235 have no unsolved problems after 32 attempts and 85 have a nonzero unsolved fraction (Figure 2). All 80 Base 10 addition conditions have zero unsolved fraction; Base 7 multiplication has a mean of 0.40, with 33 of 80 conditions above 0.5. The dependence on digit count varies across models, including nonmonotonic behavior at low digit counts for GPT-OSS-120B. Large retry gains appear around Pass@1 values of 0.05–0.35 (Figure 3), where repeated attempts can cover many initially missed problems.

First-attempt accuracy alone does not determine the gain from retries. On Base 7 addition at n=3n=3, R1-1.5B rises from Pass@1 of 0.08 to Pass@32 of 0.98, leaving E^​(32)=0.02\hat{E}(32)=0.02. On Base 7 multiplication at n≥7n\geq 7, the same model has Pass@1 of zero and E^​(32)=1\hat{E}(32)=1. R1-14B at n=6n=6 on Base 7 multiplication starts at Pass@1 of 0.14 but solves 84% of the evaluated problems with the same total sampling budget of 32 complete-answer attempts (Figure 8).

A low Pass@1 can therefore accompany either substantial retry gains or no observed success within the available budget. The observations concern finite pools of complete answers: E^​(32)>0\hat{E}(32)>0 does not identify a permanent failure floor, and digit count is not the number of checked intermediate states. Appendix D and Appendix E give the curves, mixture fits, and token counts.

4.5 Agent Score Prediction

We also examine whether a repeated-attempt curve can predict later agent scores from early observations. The retry curve approaches a fitted score ceiling with diminishing gains; a sigmoid in log time provides an alternative model of bounded score growth (Appendix F.1).

EdgeBench (Zhu et al., 2026) supplies complete observations at 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12 hours for 252 task–model pairs across five models and 51 tasks. For each target pair, we fit its 2-hour and 4-hour scores using category-level priors from other tasks. Priors exclude all model trajectories of the target task.

Median relative errors for the retry and sigmoid curves are 3.8% and 3.9% at 6 hours, increasing to 10.7% and 10.9% at 12 hours. Relative-error summaries use 248 pairs with positive observed scores at each prediction time, while all 252 pairs receive predictions. Table 6 reports all four horizons and the fractions below 10% and 20% relative error. Neither curve has the lower median error at every horizon; the retry curve has at least as many predictions below 10% error and more below 20% at each horizon. The two curves have similar prediction errors, although their priors constrain different parameters. The forecast does not identify internal checks or state reuse, or test savings from early stopping.

5 Related Work

Reasoning compositionality and long-horizon reliability.

Prior work documents difficulties composing intermediate results (Dziri et al., 2023), falling success with task duration (Kwa et al., 2025), and failures at high problem complexity (Shojaee et al., 2025). Zhang et al. (2025b) formulate compute and accuracy laws, measure compositionality gaps, and introduce SFT-Compo as a training intervention. We use their LoRe-Compo setting to study test-time sampling and state reuse.

Decomposition, search, and local error correction.

Hierarchical reinforcement learning composes subgoals through options, MAXQ, and skill chaining (Sutton et al., 1999; Dietterich, 2000; Konidaris and Barto, 2009). Least-to-Most prompting uses earlier answers to solve later subproblems (Zhou et al., 2023); Tree of Thoughts searches and backtracks over partial states (Yao et al., 2023), and Graph of Thoughts combines and refines intermediate results (Besta et al., 2024). Chain-in-Tree chains routine steps and reuses generated children when branching becomes necessary (Li, 2026). Recursive and agentic inference systems similarly pass subcall outputs to later computations (Zhang et al., 2025a; Alzu’bi et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2025; Nielsen et al., 2025). MAKER (Meyerson et al., 2025) combines extreme decomposition, error detection, and first-to-kk-ahead voting, with asymptotic foundations in Meyerson and Qiu (2025). Under its voting model, MAKER derives logarithmic voting budgets and Θ⁡(N​log⁡N)\Theta(N\log N) total expected cost for fixed task reliability, assuming local success probability above one half. Our finite-cap analysis bounds work across correct and incorrect states under first acceptance and global stopping; its cost guarantee requires precision and acceptance bounds only at correct prefixes.

Stopped testing and restart analysis.

Start-up demonstration tests study total-success and consecutive-failure stopping criteria, including dependent trials (Gera, 2013; Balakrishnan et al., 2014). Our result bounds expected work uniformly over the specified retry class and relates it to correctness at retained prefixes. Classical restart scheduling optimizes repeated complete runs (Luby et al., 1993); the present cap and stopping rule are fixed. Appendix B.10.6 gives the comparison and exact work recursion.

Verification and test-time sampling.

Independent sampling improves candidate coverage (Brown et al., 2024), while adaptive test-time computation allocates effort according to task difficulty and verification quality (Snell et al., 2025; Setlur et al., 2025; Misaki et al., 2025). Self-consistency uses answer agreement as a proxy for correctness (Wang et al., 2022); process supervision and reward models assess intermediate reasoning (Uesato et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025b). ProcessBench and Socratic-PRMBench document limits of identifying and evaluating reasoning errors (Zheng et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025). Formal verification and autoformalization provide stronger, domain-specific checks (Leino, 2010; Szegedy, 2020). Our empirical Oracle is reference-answer matching, and SC is thresholded modal-answer selection; neither verifies a full reasoning trace. Labiad et al. (2026) train a search policy to guide a frozen answer model and show that gains over repeated sampling depend on decoding and exploration choices. Their comparisons match the answer-generation allocation; concept generation adds a small separate inference cost. Our arithmetic experiments measure repeated-answer coverage under fixed decoding.

Retained context and execution cost.

Atom of Thoughts decomposes and contracts problems into self-contained states designed to preserve answer equivalence (Teng et al., 2025). MEM1 learns a compact recurrent state and discards redundant interaction history (Zhou et al., 2025). These methods address what to retain. Our analysis specifies the correctness and continuation conditions that the retained state must satisfy. Using counterfactual error histories, Sinha et al. (2025) show that earlier mistakes can impair later reasoning, with thinking mitigating this effect in their experiments. Context length and information placement can also affect model behavior (Liu et al., 2024). Adaptive sequential Monte Carlo avoids recomputing shared prefixes by reordering KV caches and particle tensors during resampling (Wang et al., 2026). This reduces execution cost without establishing the correctness of retained reasoning. Appendix A.1 gives a separate qualitative recurrence. The reliability proof instead controls errors at correct prefixes and bounds the probability of retaining an incorrect intermediate state.

6 Discussion

Acceptance and correctness.

At a fixed retained state, more attempts increase the chance that a candidate passes the check. With the same candidate distribution and check, they leave the error rate among accepted candidates unchanged. Reliable continuation therefore requires both a sufficiently accurate check and a state that contains the information needed by later steps. Checking an answer and retaining its full reasoning trace impose different correctness requirements on what is passed forward.

Executed work and total cost.

The local cap reserves enough attempts for difficult steps, while acceptance often allows the procedure to advance earlier. With constant acceptance probability and sufficient precision, the stopped loop uses linearly many attempts in expectation. The cost of generating candidates, checking them, and processing retained states must then be counted at every reached state. A stricter check can improve precision while increasing the cost of each attempt or reducing the chance of acceptance. Both effects enter the comparison between checking cost and avoided generation.

Choosing a sampling configuration.

The arithmetic results show that the benefit of more attempts varies across tasks, even when first-attempt accuracy is low. On the paired mathematics problems, the answer-only prompt scores closer to full context than to no context, although the comparison changes instructions as well as retained information. Larger candidate and continuation budgets also give uneven gains across models. These observations help describe the configurations evaluated here. Establishing computational savings from reuse still requires a comparison at the same whole-task success rate, with generation, checking, and retained-state processing all included.

7 Conclusion

Reliable reuse depends on which candidates a check accepts and how later steps use the retained state. Under the stated retry and stopping rules, we give conditions for correct completion and bounds on executed attempts. Additional retries reduce exhaustion, while the candidate distribution and check determine accepted-state precision. Total cost depends on per-attempt cost and acceptance probability.

The experiments document second-subproblem coverage across continuation prompts and variable gains from repeated arithmetic answers. They describe practical sampling choices but do not establish the long-chain guarantees. Assessing reuse on a new task requires measuring retained-state error, continuation reliability, and total cost at matched whole-task success.

Limitations

Execution and checking assumptions.

The work theorem assumes conditionally independent, identically distributed retries at each retained state and termination when the local budget is exhausted. Feedback that changes the next attempt and fallback after exhaustion require separate analysis. The binary-check examples further assume that check outcomes are independent conditional on candidate correctness. The experiments do not directly test these execution assumptions.

Checks and retained information.

Agreement can select common correct answers, but shared errors can also receive many votes (Wang et al., 2022). Similar SC and Oracle scores on the second subproblem do not tell us how often either selector keeps a wrong first answer. The correctness condition applies to everything passed forward: checking an extracted answer does not verify a reasoning trace retained alongside it. Process-verifier benchmarks document errors in learned checks; formal verification uses task-specific correctness criteria (Zheng et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025; Leino, 2010; Szegedy, 2020).

Decomposition and empirical scope.

The theorem takes the decomposition and correctness criterion as inputs. A smaller step can be easier to check but requires more checks; a larger step may retain information whose correctness is harder to establish. The LoRe-Compo subproblems are mathematically separate, and arithmetic retries whole answers, so neither experiment estimates uniform reliability at the prefixes of a long dependent chain. Open-ended tasks may need different representations and task-specific checks before the sufficient conditions become applicable. The available composite aggregates do not identify accepted-state error or fallback contributions; prompt differences also prevent isolating an information-reuse effect.

Cost and auxiliary models.

The total-cost bound includes generation, checking, and state processing at every reached state. Growing contexts or more accurate checks can increase that cost and must remain explicit in the budget expression. When complete solutions are already reliable, the extra checking may outweigh the work saved by reuse. The appendix’s qualitative error-propagation and mixture models describe possible behaviors; finite retry pools cannot identify a permanent capability boundary. Agent-score prediction also does not identify internal verification or establish a compute-allocation benefit.

AI Use Statement

We used generative AI tools to assist manuscript writing, revision, and the development and checking of mathematical derivations. The language models used to generate candidate solutions and continuations, together with the answer-selection procedures, are part of the experimental protocols described in Section 4. We take responsibility for the final manuscript and its scientific claims.

Appendix A Modeling Assumptions and Their Scope

The analysis uses explicit assumptions about sampling, checks, and task decomposition. This appendix states their scope and relates them to the experimental protocols. The Limitations section explains their implications for checking, continuation, and empirical interpretation.

Independence assumption (see Limitations).

Prop. 3 requires matching subproblem success rates between composite and standalone prompts, within-run independence of subproblem correctness, and independent identically distributed composite runs. The reuse result in Prop. 5 requires the same reliability bounds for every correct accepted state passed to later stages, with the total bound on accepted-state errors below the target failure probability. Our experiments sample subproblem pairs from distinct MATH subjects as a practical way to reduce concept overlap between subproblems. Subject separation does not establish these assumptions: shared formatting, latent correlations, and position-dependent generation can affect both dependence and marginal success rates.

Error propagation assumptions (see Limitations).

The error model in Appendix A.1 assumes that earlier failures add linearly to later failure probabilities, remain in context, and have a common baseline probability qtclean=q¯q_{t}^{\mathrm{clean}}=\bar{q} when preceding steps are correct. Real autoregressive models exhibit nonlinear error interactions, heterogeneous step difficulty, and partial attention decay across long contexts [Liu et al., 2024], none of which the closed-form solution q¯​(1+cctx)t−1\bar{q}(1{+}c_{\mathrm{ctx}})^{t-1} captures. Appendix A.1 gives the closed form; its parameters are not fitted to the experimental data.

Stepwise decomposition requirement (see Limitations).

Prop. 5 requires each step to have a positive probability of producing a correct accepted state from every correct input state. A suitable decomposition must keep the individual steps within the model’s capabilities. Open-ended generation, planning without intermediate checks, and tasks without a step-level correctness criterion may not admit such a decomposition, so the product lower bound need not apply.

Task length must reflect reasoning steps.

The scaling variable NN counts steps in the chosen decomposition, rather than prompt length or operand digits. Memorization or familiarity can let a model answer without following that decomposition, changing the relation between input size and executed work. Comparing Base 7 and Base 10 varies the numeral representation; without observations of internal steps, it cannot determine the process used to obtain an answer.

Reliability of checks (see Limitations).

On LoRe-Compo, self-consistency (SC) and Oracle selection yield similar second-subproblem success rates. This comparison does not estimate the accuracy of either check, and the arithmetic experiments do not compare these selection rules. The error rate among accepted SC answers can be measured by comparing them with reference answers, excluding fallback candidates that did not pass the check. Summaries that include fallback continuations describe all retained paths and cannot directly estimate the error rate among accepted states.

A.1 Error Propagation Model

Errors in autoregressive generation may remain in the input context and affect later steps [Zhang et al., 2023, Liu et al., 2024]. Let qtq_{t} be the failure probability at step tt under the generated prefix, and qtcleanq_{t}^{\mathrm{clean}} its value when all preceding steps are correct. For a coefficient cctx≥0c_{\mathrm{ctx}}\geq 0 describing the effect of earlier errors, consider the qualitative approximation

qt≈qtclean+cctx​∑j<tqj.q_{t}\;\approx\;q_{t}^{\mathrm{clean}}+c_{\mathrm{ctx}}\sum_{j<t}q_{j}. (11)

If qtclean=q¯q_{t}^{\mathrm{clean}}=\bar{q} at every step, differencing the recurrence gives

qt≈q¯​(1+cctx)t−1.q_{t}\;\approx\;\bar{q}(1+c_{\mathrm{ctx}})^{t-1}. (12)

When q¯>0\bar{q}>0 and cctx>0c_{\mathrm{ctx}}>0, this expression increases with the step index. If the baseline difficulty varies across steps, cctx>0c_{\mathrm{ctx}}>0 alone does not imply increasing failure probability. The parameters cctxc_{\mathrm{ctx}} and q¯\bar{q} are not fitted here. The recurrence is a qualitative approximation with a linear, persistent context effect, valid only while predicted probabilities remain below one. The recurrence offers an intuition for context-carried errors, while the product comparison and reuse guarantee use their own explicit probability assumptions. Arithmetic retries do not observe step failures within a run and cannot directly test this recurrence.

A.2 Correct Candidates before Checking

For a fixed step instance and correct input state ss, let pt​(s)p_{t}(s) be the probability that a generated candidate is correct before checking. With RR independent identically distributed attempts from this fixed context, the probability of no correct candidate is (1−pt​(s))R(1-p_{t}(s))^{R}, which tends to zero whenever pt​(s)>0p_{t}(s)>0. Across a distribution of step instances and correct input states, define the probability of generating no correct candidate and its asymptotic error floor by

qtclean​(R):=𝔼s​[(1−pt​(s))R],qtfloor:=limR→∞qtclean​(R)=Ps​(pt​(s)=0).q_{t}^{\mathrm{clean}}(R):=\mathbb{E}_{s}\!\left[(1-p_{t}(s))^{R}\right],\qquad q_{t}^{\mathrm{floor}}:=\lim_{R\to\infty}q_{t}^{\mathrm{clean}}(R)=P_{s}(p_{t}(s)=0). (13)

The limit follows by bounded convergence; a nonzero floor can arise from positive mass on locally unsolvable instances, rather than from independent retries at a fixed positive success probability. A two-component approximation assigns mass qtfloorq_{t}^{\mathrm{floor}} to such instances and uses a common failure probability εloc,t∈[0,1)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{loc},t}\in[0,1) for the remaining instances:

qtclean​(R)≈qtfloor+(1−qtfloor)​εloc,tR.q_{t}^{\mathrm{clean}}(R)\;\approx\;q_{t}^{\mathrm{floor}}+(1-q_{t}^{\mathrm{floor}})\varepsilon_{\mathrm{loc},t}^{R}. (14)

This expression is exact for the stated two-point mixture; independence alone does not imply this mixture or a common failure probability on solvable instances. Its zero-floor special case is

qtfloor=0⟹qtclean​(R)≈εloc,tR.q_{t}^{\mathrm{floor}}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q_{t}^{\mathrm{clean}}(R)\approx\varepsilon_{\mathrm{loc},t}^{R}. (15)

These probabilities concern generated candidates before checking. They do not include the effect of accepting an incorrect candidate or rejecting a correct one. The arithmetic experiments in Section 4.4 use complete-answer attempts. The unsolved fraction at R=32R=32 neither identifies an asymptotic error floor nor estimates the theorem’s per-step failure probability.

Appendix B Proofs and Supporting Analysis

This appendix gives the formal results and their proofs. It covers complete-solution sampling, retry budgets, stage composition, and stopped state reuse. Each result specifies its assumptions.

B.1 Setup and Notation

We use the same model notation throughout the paper: 𝜽\bm{\theta} denotes the parameters of the reasoning model, and p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}} denotes its induced generation distribution. For a problem xx, fix a decomposition into N≥1N\geq 1 steps and write a sampled reasoning chain as z1:N=(z1,…,zN)z_{1:N}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{N}), where ztz_{t} is the text generated at step tt. Let st=[x,z1:t]s_{t}=[x,z_{1:t}] denote the full generated history after step tt, with s0=xs_{0}=x. In reuse, sts_{t} instead denotes the task information and intermediate results actually passed forward, as in Section 2; the prompt presents this state to the model. Each step is sampled autoregressively from p𝜽(⋅∣st−1)p_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot\mid s_{t-1}). The final answer yy is extracted from the completed run. The reuse result assumes that correct completion of every stage yields a correct final answer: if every accepted state is correct and all stages terminate, extraction returns the composite target (for two stages, [a⋆​(x1),a⋆​(x2)][a^{\star}(x_{1}),a^{\star}(x_{2})]; likewise for multiple stages below). Correctness refers to the retained state, not to reasoning discarded during answer extraction. For local step analysis, 𝒢t​(st−1,zt)∈{0,1}\mathcal{G}_{t}(s_{t-1},z_{t})\in\{0,1\} indicates whether the resulting state is correct, qt:=P⁡(𝒢t=0)q_{t}:=P(\mathcal{G}_{t}=0) is its failure probability, and qtcleanq_{t}^{\mathrm{clean}} is the corresponding probability when all preceding states are correct. The check 𝒱t​(st−1,zt)∈{0,1}\mathcal{V}_{t}(s_{t-1},z_{t})\in\{0,1\} separately records rejection or acceptance and may disagree with 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t}. We write N⁡(x)N(x) for the length of the chosen decomposition of xx, abbreviated as NN when the problem is clear. The single-run quantities are C𝜽,1​(x)=𝔼​[L]C_{\bm{\theta},1}(x)=\mathbb{E}[L] and A𝜽,1​(x)=P⁡(y=a⋆​(x))A_{\bm{\theta},1}(x)=P(y=a^{\star}(x)), where LL is the total generated token count. For two subproblems x1,x2x_{1},x_{2}, their composition x1⊕x2x_{1}\oplus x_{2} is formed by concatenating them with a connector prompt. We define its composite target as a⋆​(x1⊕x2):=[a⋆​(x1),a⋆​(x2)]a^{\star}(x_{1}\oplus x_{2}):=[a^{\star}(x_{1}),a^{\star}(x_{2})]. For these chosen decompositions, step-count additivity means that the step counts satisfy

N⁡(x1⊕x2)=N⁡(x1)+N⁡(x2).N(x_{1}\oplus x_{2})=N(x_{1})+N(x_{2}). (16)

Operationally, our experiments use distinct MATH subjects as a practical proxy for reduced concept overlap across subproblems. Step-count additivity does not imply the marginal-matching or probabilistic independence assumptions of Prop. 3. For reuse, a step must admit independent repeated attempts from a fixed input state and an accept-or-reject check 𝒱\mathcal{V}. The ideal predicate 𝒢\mathcal{G} defines correctness, whereas 𝒱\mathcal{V} is the check applied to candidate states; acceptance alone does not imply 𝒢=1\mathcal{G}=1. In the reuse proofs, 0<ρ<10<\rho<1 uniformly bounds ρt​(s)\rho_{t}(s), and α\alpha uniformly bounds the error rate αt​(R,s)\alpha_{t}(R;s) among accepted states over all relevant steps, correct accepted input states ss, and attempt budgets RR. With RR total attempts, equivalently R−1R{-}1 retries, all candidates are rejected with probability at most ρR\rho^{R}. Returning an incorrect accepted state is a separate source of failure. For independent sampling, the accuracy and generation cost of KK complete runs satisfy

A𝜽,K​(x)\displaystyle A_{\bm{\theta},K}(x) =1−(1−A𝜽,1​(x))K\displaystyle=1-(1-A_{\bm{\theta},1}(x))^{K} (17)
C𝜽,K​(x)\displaystyle C_{\bm{\theta},K}(x) =K⋅C𝜽,1​(x)\displaystyle=K\cdot C_{\bm{\theta},1}(x) (18)

Here A𝜽,KA_{\bm{\theta},K} is Pass@KK coverage and C𝜽,KC_{\bm{\theta},K} is expected generation cost; K=1K=1 denotes a single complete run. Across task lengths NN, the conditional scaling assumptions are

C𝜽,1​(x)\displaystyle C_{\bm{\theta},1}(x) =Θ(N)(Compute Law)\displaystyle=\Theta(N)\quad\text{(Compute Law)} (19)
A𝜽,1​(x)\displaystyle A_{\bm{\theta},1}(x) =exp(−λ𝜽N),λ𝜽>0(Accuracy Law)\displaystyle=\exp(-\lambda_{\bm{\theta}}N),\quad\lambda_{\bm{\theta}}>0\quad\text{(Accuracy Law)} (20)
Notation conventions.

All probabilities denoted by P⁡(⋅)P(\cdot) are taken under the relevant sampling process induced by p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}}; p𝜽p_{\bm{\theta}} itself denotes the model distribution. For an integer KK, [K][K] denotes {1,…,K}\{1,\ldots,K\}. The symbol ⋘\lll denotes an informal “much smaller than” condition in limiting approximations. Failure budgets satisfy δ,δi,δm∈(0,1)\delta,\delta_{i},\delta_{m}\in(0,1), with δ=δ1+δ2\delta=\delta_{1}+\delta_{2} in the two-stage result and ∑mδm=δ\sum_{m}\delta_{m}=\delta in the multi-stage result, where the sum ranges over all stages of the task.

B.2 Ideal Laws Under Per-Step Errors

We begin with the success probability and cost implied by independent per-step errors. This calculation concerns a step decomposition; the arithmetic experiments measure complete-answer coverage.

Proof.

Step 1: Success requires all steps. Let FiF_{i} indicate failure at step ii; each step succeeds with probability 1−ε1-\varepsilon, so independence yields the following product:

A𝜽,1​(x)=∏i=1NP⁡(Fi=0)=(1−ε)N.A_{\bm{\theta},1}(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{N}P(F_{i}=0)=(1-\varepsilon)^{N}. (22)

Step 2: Logarithmic inequality. Since log\log is concave and log⁡(1)=0\log(1)=0, the tangent line at x=1x=1 gives log⁡(x)≤x−1\log(x)\leq x-1 for all x>0x>0. Substituting x=1−εx=1-\varepsilon: log⁡(1−ε)≤(1−ε)−1=−ε\log(1-\varepsilon)\leq(1-\varepsilon)-1=-\varepsilon for all ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1). Taking the natural logarithm of Step 1:

log⁡A𝜽,1​(x)=N​log⁡(1−ε)≤−ε​N.\log A_{\bm{\theta},1}(x)=N\log(1-\varepsilon)\leq-\varepsilon N. (23)

Step 3: Exponential bound and approximation. Exponentiating both sides:

A𝜽,1​(x)≤e−ε​N.A_{\bm{\theta},1}(x)\leq e^{-\varepsilon N}. (24)

For fixed NN as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, the Taylor expansion log⁡(1−ε)=−ε+O⁡(ε2)\log(1-\varepsilon)=-\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^{2}) yields A𝜽,1​(x)/e−ε​N→1A_{\bm{\theta},1}(x)/e^{-\varepsilon N}\to 1. ∎

B.3 The Compositionality Breakdown under Independent Sampling

We first give a general event-inclusion bound for a common pool of composite runs, then prove the conditional product comparison used in the main text.

Proof of Prop. 2.

For a pool of KK composite runs with sample space Ω\Omega, define

E12K\displaystyle E_{12}^{K} :={∃k:run ​k​ returns a correct answer to both ​x1​ and ​x2},\displaystyle:=\{\exists k:\text{run }k\text{ returns a correct answer to both }x_{1}\text{ and }x_{2}\}, (27)
E1K\displaystyle E_{1}^{K} :={∃k:run ​k​ returns a correct answer to ​x1},\displaystyle:=\{\exists k:\text{run }k\text{ returns a correct answer to }x_{1}\},

and analogously E2KE_{2}^{K} for x2x_{2}. The inclusion E12K⊆E1K∩E2KE_{12}^{K}\subseteq E_{1}^{K}\cap E_{2}^{K} holds: if some run kk is correct on both subproblems, then that same run witnesses E1KE_{1}^{K} and witnesses E2KE_{2}^{K}. Monotonicity of probability gives P⁡(E12K)≤P⁡(E1K∩E2K)≤min⁡{P⁡(E1K),P⁡(E2K)}P(E_{12}^{K})\leq P(E_{1}^{K}\cap E_{2}^{K})\leq\min\{P(E_{1}^{K}),P(E_{2}^{K})\}, which is Eq. (25). This bound holds for every KK without assuming independence of subproblem-answer correctness. ∎

Proof of Prop. 3.

Assume the matching composite/standalone marginals, within-run independence, and across-run i.i.d. conditions, and let a:=A𝜽,1​(x1)a:=A_{\bm{\theta},1}(x_{1}) and b:=A𝜽,1​(x2)b:=A_{\bm{\theta},1}(x_{2}), so that A𝜽,1​(x1⊕x2)=a​bA_{\bm{\theta},1}(x_{1}\oplus x_{2})=ab. For KK independently sampled runs, define indicator random variables: Xk∈{0,1}X_{k}\in\{0,1\} records that sampled run kk succeeds on x1x_{1} with P⁡(Xk=1)=aP(X_{k}=1)=a; Yk∈{0,1}Y_{k}\in\{0,1\} records that sampled run kk succeeds on x2x_{2} with P⁡(Yk=1)=bP(Y_{k}=1)=b; and Zk:=Xk​YkZ_{k}:=X_{k}Y_{k} records that sampled run kk succeeds on both with P⁡(Zk=1)=a​bP(Z_{k}=1)=ab. The two sequences are independent, with i.i.d. entries within each sequence.

Step 1: Event formulation. Define success events:

E1K:={∃k:Xk=1},E2K:={∃k:Yk=1},E12K:={∃k:Zk=1}.E_{1}^{K}:=\{\exists k:X_{k}=1\},\quad E_{2}^{K}:=\{\exists k:Y_{k}=1\},\quad E_{12}^{K}:=\{\exists k:Z_{k}=1\}. (28)

Independence across runs gives the following probabilities for the three success events:

P⁡(E1K)=1−(1−a)K,P⁡(E2K)=1−(1−b)K,P⁡(E12K)=1−(1−a​b)K.P(E_{1}^{K})=1-(1-a)^{K},\quad P(E_{2}^{K})=1-(1-b)^{K},\quad P(E_{12}^{K})=1-(1-ab)^{K}. (29)

Step 2: Set inclusion. Key observation: E12K⊆E1K∩E2KE_{12}^{K}\subseteq E_{1}^{K}\cap E_{2}^{K}. To see this, suppose ζ∈E12K\zeta\in E_{12}^{K}, so there exists kk with Zk​(ζ)=Xk​(ζ)​Yk​(ζ)=1Z_{k}(\zeta)=X_{k}(\zeta)Y_{k}(\zeta)=1. Then Xk​(ζ)=1X_{k}(\zeta)=1, hence ζ∈E1K\zeta\in E_{1}^{K}; and Yk​(ζ)=1Y_{k}(\zeta)=1, hence ζ∈E2K\zeta\in E_{2}^{K}. Therefore ζ∈E1K∩E2K\zeta\in E_{1}^{K}\cap E_{2}^{K}, completing the inclusion. Monotonicity of probability gives:

P⁡(E12K)≤P⁡(E1K∩E2K).P(E_{12}^{K})\leq P(E_{1}^{K}\cap E_{2}^{K}). (30)

Step 3: Independence gives exact product. Since {Xk}k=1K\{X_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} and {Yk}k=1K\{Y_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} are mutually independent by assumption, any event measurable w.r.t. {Xk}\{X_{k}\} alone is independent of any event measurable w.r.t. {Yk}\{Y_{k}\} alone. E1K={∃k:Xk=1}E_{1}^{K}=\{\exists k:X_{k}=1\} depends only on {Xk}\{X_{k}\}, and E2K={∃k:Yk=1}E_{2}^{K}=\{\exists k:Y_{k}=1\} depends only on {Yk}\{Y_{k}\}. Therefore E1KE_{1}^{K} and E2KE_{2}^{K} are independent:

P⁡(E1K∩E2K)=P⁡(E1K)​P​(E2K)=[1−(1−a)K]​[1−(1−b)K].P(E_{1}^{K}\cap E_{2}^{K})=P(E_{1}^{K})P(E_{2}^{K})=[1-(1-a)^{K}][1-(1-b)^{K}]. (31)

Combining this product identity with the event inclusion from Step 2 gives the comparison

1−(1−a​b)K≤[1−(1−a)K]​[1−(1−b)K].1-(1-ab)^{K}\leq[1-(1-a)^{K}][1-(1-b)^{K}]. (32)

This establishes the non-strict product comparison in Prop. 3; strictness is proved next.

Step 4: Strictness. For K≥2K\geq 2 and a,b∈(0,1)a,b\in(0,1), the inequality is strict. Consider the event:

E1,2:={X1=1,Y1=0,X2=0,Y2=1,∀k≥3:XkYk=0}.E_{1,2}:=\{X_{1}=1,\;Y_{1}=0,\;X_{2}=0,\;Y_{2}=1,\;\forall\,k\geq 3:\;X_{k}Y_{k}=0\}. (33)

The following three properties show that this event has positive mass outside joint success.

(i) E1,2⊆E1K∩E2KE_{1,2}\subseteq E_{1}^{K}\cap E_{2}^{K}. X1=1X_{1}=1 implies E1KE_{1}^{K}; Y2=1Y_{2}=1 implies E2KE_{2}^{K}.

Hence no sampled run succeeds on both subproblems, so E12KE_{12}^{K} does not occur under this construction.

(iii) P⁡(E1,2)>0P(E_{1,2})>0. By mutual independence of all {Xk}\{X_{k}\} and {Yk}\{Y_{k}\}:

P⁡(E1,2)=a⁡(1−b)​(1−a)​b​∏k=3K(1−a​b)=a​b​(1−a)​(1−b)​(1−a​b)K−2>0,P(E_{1,2})=a(1-b)(1-a)b\prod_{k=3}^{K}(1-ab)=ab(1-a)(1-b)(1-ab)^{K-2}>0, (34)

The strict positivity follows because every factor is positive for a,b∈(0,1)a,b\in(0,1).

Properties (i) and (ii) give E1,2⊆(E1K∩E2K)∖E12KE_{1,2}\subseteq(E_{1}^{K}\cap E_{2}^{K})\setminus E_{12}^{K}, so P⁡((E1K∩E2K)∖E12K)≥P⁡(E1,2)>0P((E_{1}^{K}\cap E_{2}^{K})\setminus E_{12}^{K})\geq P(E_{1,2})>0, establishing the required strict comparison P⁡(E12K)<P⁡(E1K∩E2K)P(E_{12}^{K})<P(E_{1}^{K}\cap E_{2}^{K}) for every K≥2K\geq 2. ∎

Low accuracy behavior in the difficult problem range.

Under the assumptions of Prop. 3, consider the ratio between composite accuracy and the product of standalone accuracies when K​a,K​b⋘1Ka,Kb\lll 1. The approximation 1−(1−x)K≈K​x1-(1-x)^{K}\approx Kx for K​x⋘1Kx\lll 1 follows from (1−x)K=1−K​x+O⁡(K2​x2)(1-x)^{K}=1-Kx+O(K^{2}x^{2}). Applying this to each term:

A𝜽,K​(x1)\displaystyle A_{\bm{\theta},K}(x_{1}) =1−(1−a)K≈K​a,A𝜽,K​(x2)=1−(1−b)K≈K​b,\displaystyle=1-(1-a)^{K}\approx Ka,\quad A_{\bm{\theta},K}(x_{2})=1-(1-b)^{K}\approx Kb,
